Lateral gradients prepared in aluminum oxide cast FTC slurries. 21 Discussions with OCOchem established that while ceramics provided an inert framework to support OCOchem’s tin and bismuth oxide catalyst particles, the non- compliant nature of the ceramic materials posed a challenge with the integration in OCOchem test beds. Polymers and/or metals were needed to provide the compliance needed to integrate the FTC membranes into test systems, so research progressed in evaluating alternate materials. Acrylic was successfully cast and sintered into a rigid yet compliance structure that could be easily integrated into a test frame (Figure 10); however, the acrylic's poor electronic conductivity was problematic for maintaining an electrical current pathway to the catalyst particles entrained in the carbon paper to which the membrane would be laminated. “Sintered” sample Acrylic -10x10cm cast Green Figure 10. FTC cast acrylic, dyed red for simple observation of the structure, demonstrating sufficient strength and compliance. Metallic particles were recognized as the ideal material for the membrane that could achieve electrical conductivity in excess of the carbon paper. While powder metallurgy approaches can yield sintering scenarios similar to ceramic or polymer particles, achieving stable slurries with high-density particles with a propensity to settle requires new slurry formulation and dispersants. However, silver oxide (Ag O) represented a 2 unique opportunity to demonstrate the freeze-cast structure in metallic materials (Figure 11). Silver oxide disperses and casts like a traditional ceramic oxide; however, above 300C, the silver oxide reduces to metallic silver in the air. 22 Figure 11. FTC cast silver oxide (left) sintered in air to silver metal (middle), demonstrating superb compliance and strength (right). The carbon paper that OCOchem utilizes for catalyst support, measured with an inductance (L), capacitance (C), and resistance (R) (LCR) meter, yielded a conductivity of ~1.3x10-3 S/cm. However, the silver cast at 10% solids loading (i.e., porosity near 90%) demonstrated a superb conductivity up to 5.5x104 S/cm.
